parole.significato: A Filipino faith healer or witch doctor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog albularyo, from Spanish herbolario (“herbalist”).

parole.significato: Traditional Philippine stickfighting, a martial art.
parole.testo: From Tagalog arnis, from Spanish arnés in the archaic sense of “a chivalric set of weapons or armor” (compare English harness).

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to Batangas.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Batangueño, from Spanish batangueño, from Batangas + -eño.

parole.significato: A Filipino dish consisting of thinly-sliced beefsteak braised in soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, ground black peppe…
parole.testo: From Tagalog bistek, from Spanish bistec, from English beefsteak. Doublet of beefsteak and bifshtek.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to Cavite.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Caviteño, from Spanish caviteño, from Cavite + -eño.

parole.significato: A kind of dwarf or goblin in Filipino folklore.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog duwende, from Spanish duende (“goblin, elf”). Doublet of duende.

parole.significato: Synonym of ensaimada.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog ensaymada, from Spanish ensaimada, from Catalan ensaïmada. Doublet of ensaimada.

parole.significato: The traditional martial arts of the Philippines, which emphasize the use of sticks, knives, and various improvised weap…
parole.testo: From Tagalog escrima or eskrima, borrowed from Spanish esgrima, noun form of the verb esgrimir (“to handle a melee weapon whether for offensive or defensive purposes”).

parole.significato: A flaky pastry (typically filled with either mung bean, pork bits, purple yam, azuki bean, or etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog hopia, from Spanish hopia, from Hokkien, possibly 好餅 /好饼 (hó piáⁿ, literally “good pastry”) according to Chan-Yap (1980) and Manuel (1948). See also Early Manila Hokkien 香餅 /香饼 (hioⁿ-piáⁿ, literally “fragrant pastry”), Indonesian bakpia. Compare Cebuano hopya.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Iloilo.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Ilonggo, from Spanish ilongo, from ilong + -o, the root referring to Hiligaynon ilong (“nose”), from the nose-like shape of the land between the Iloilo River and Batiano River where the Spanish Fort San Pedro is located. See also Spanish pampango.

parole.significato: A goat stew from the Philippines, commonly made with vegetables and liver paste.
parole.testo: From Tagalog kaldereta, from Spanish caldereta, from caldero + -eta.

parole.significato: A male American.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog Kano, initial clipping of Amerikano, ultimately from Spanish americano (“male American”).

parole.significato: steamed and pan-fried elongated beancurd rolls over meatloaves of meat (usually ground pork) and vegetables, served as…
parole.testo: From Tagalog kikiam or Spanish que-quian, from Hokkien, possibly 雞 /鸡 (ke, “chicken”) + 繭 /茧 (kián, “cocoon”) or 鹹 /咸 (kiâm, “viand; rice topping”). See also kiampong, tawkiam, Hokkien 鹹飯 /咸饭 (kiâm-pn̄g) and Taiwanese Hokkien 雞卷 /鸡卷 (koe-kńg), 肉繭 /肉茧, 肉繭仔 /肉茧仔, 繭仔 /茧仔, Cebuano ngohiong, Cebuano temp

parole.significato: bird's nest soup (Chinese soup made from edible bird's nest)
parole.testo: From Tagalog nido (“edible bird's nest”) + soup. Tagalog nido itself is from Spanish nido (“nest”). See also El Nido in Palawan, where the edible bird's nest is historically harvested from by a Busyador.

parole.significato: An ornamental star-like Christmas lantern from the Philippines.
parole.testo: From Tagalog parol, from Spanish farol (“lantern”).

parole.significato: A skirt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog saya, from Spanish saya.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Tayabas, Quezon.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Tayabense, from Spanish tayabense, from Tayabas + -ense.

parole.significato: A person from Quezon and Aurora provinces.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Tayabeño, from Spanish tayabeño, from Tayabas + -eño.

parole.significato: An aunt; auntie.
parole.testo: From Tagalog tita, from Spanish tita.

parole.significato: An uncle.
parole.testo: From Tagalog tito, from Spanish tito.

parole.significato: A Philippine omelette of ground meat and potatoes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog torta, from Spanish torta, from Latin turta, thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”). Doublet of torte and tart.

parole.significato: corrupt politician
parole.testo: Contraction of traditional politician; also influenced by Tagalog trapo (“rag”), from Spanish trapo.

parole.significato: A Philippine snack made of a fried and caramelized spring roll wrapping thinly sliced bananas.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog turon, from Spanish turrón.
